title: Relative strength: leading compared with what?
subtitle: Separate winning the comparison from making money.
takeaway: Outperformance is a relative statement. A stock can lead its benchmark while both lose value.

sections.title: A comparison always needs a second object
paragraphs: Suppose your stock rises 5%. That sounds strong until you learn its sector rose 15%. Now suppose it falls 5% while the broad market falls 20%. The absolute result is negative, but the comparative result is stronger. Relative-strength analysis keeps these two questions separate: what happened to this stock, and what happened to it compared with an explicitly named alternative over the same interval?

Fidelity describes a relative-strength comparison as a ratio of one security’s price to another security’s or index’s price. If stock price is S and benchmark value is B, the ratio is S/B. An increase means the numerator performed better in proportional terms over the comparison. This relative-strength ratio is different from RSI, an oscillator based on a single instrument’s own gains and losses. Similar names do not imply identical calculations.

sections.title: Rebase the comparison so its origin is visible
paragraphs: A raw ratio’s level depends on price units. A $50 stock divided by a 500-point benchmark starts at 0.1; replacing that benchmark with a proportional series in different units changes the number without changing its performance. Rebase the ratio to 100 at a stated start: relative index today = 100 × (S today / B today) / (S start / B start). Now the movement has a clear comparison point.

For fictional start values S = $100 and B = 100, and end values S = $90 and B = 80, the rebased ratio is 100 × (90/80) = 112.5. The stock declined 10%, yet the ratio rose 12.5%. Subtracting returns instead yields a 10-percentage-point advantage: −10% minus −20%. The ratio’s percentage change and the return difference are distinct quantities, so label whichever you use.

tables.title: Main comparison: all series rebased at 100

sections.title: Choose a benchmark that answers your question
paragraphs: A broad market benchmark asks how the stock performed against a diversified market reference. A sector benchmark asks how it performed against a closer industry-related alternative. A peer asks a narrower comparison, but differences in size, geography, leverage, and business mix can still matter. None is universally correct. Write the question first and select the comparator deliberately rather than choosing whichever makes the stock appear strongest.

Imagine a manufacturer gains 8%, its sector gains 12%, and the broad market gains 4%. It outperformed the broad market while underperforming its sector. That pattern may motivate research into common industry conditions and company-specific differences, but the ratios alone establish neither cause. If the benchmark itself contains the stock at a large weight, the comparison also partly reflects the stock in the denominator. Recognize that overlap before interpreting the relationship.

sections.title: Use consistent dates, distributions, and units
paragraphs: Two histories must refer to comparable observations. Comparing a stock’s latest close with a stale benchmark quote can create spurious movement. Missing sessions, different trading hours, currency changes, and corporate actions also require care. A raw two-for-one split halves the quoted share price while doubling the shares held; an unadjusted ratio could falsely appear to collapse. Investor.gov’s split definition explains why this is a change in units rather than an equivalent overnight ownership loss.

A price comparison excludes distributed cash unless the history is adjusted for that purpose. A total-return comparison incorporates distributions under its stated reinvestment convention. Comparing a stock’s price return with a benchmark’s total return mixes two different measures. Use matched conventions and document the provider’s adjustment policy. For this book’s fictional illustrations, there are no distributions, currency changes, or splits, so the arithmetic remains directly visible.

sections.title: Follow the comparison chronologically
paragraphs: At session 1 all three main series are 100, so each relative index begins at 100. At session 3 the stock is 101, sector 100, and market 99. It is up 1% absolutely, ahead of sector by one percentage point and market by two. Its stock/market index is 101/99 × 100 ≈ 102.0202. The calculation uses percentage relationships; it is not a difference in quoted price units.

At session 6, stock 96 is down 4%, sector 93 down 7%, and market 90 down 10%. The stock now loses money over the interval while outperforming both references. Its relative indices are 96/93 × 100 ≈ 103.2258 against sector and 96/90 × 100 ≈ 106.6667 against market. The bottom panel rises while the top panel falls. Read both before using the word strength.

At session 12, stock 90, sector 85, and market 80 give relative indices 105.8824 and 112.5. The stock’s absolute −10% accompanies a five-percentage-point advantage over sector and ten-point advantage over market. The higher market-relative figure reflects the market’s greater weakness (80 versus the sector’s 85), not a different stock result; the stock itself did not earn +12.5%.

A precise note now says “stock declined less than both comparators in this window; its relative strength versus market exceeded that versus sector.” Sector leadership and market leadership can differ in other windows. Changing the comparator is appropriate when changing the research question, but not to rescue an unfavorable comparison after its outcome is known.

sections.title: Use the comparison to organize research
paragraphs: Return to the manufacturer from the benchmark section: stock +8%, sector +12%, market +4%. Stock/market relative index is 108/104 × 100 = 103.8462, while stock/sector is 108/112 × 100 = 96.4286. Absolute gain and market outperformance coexist with sector underperformance. This is why a “strong stock” label should identify the benchmark and period.

An investor could use these observations to decide where further business or chart research is useful. In the main dataset, ask whether relative resilience is consistent across shorter windows or concentrated around a few dates. In the contrast, ask why the sector was stronger than this company. The ratios identify the comparison; they do not by themselves establish causes or replace valuation and diversification.

For a method selecting leaders, eligibility, horizon, ranking, and rebalance rules still require explicit specification. That is a later system-design task. The beginner task here is to calculate matched comparisons and write a coherent note. Record distributions, currency, adjustment policy, and timestamps before moving from these synthetic price-only examples to a real data provider.

A quick quality check is to work backward: divide the stock growth factor by the benchmark growth factor. Main end factors are 0.90/0.80 = 1.125 and 0.90/0.85 = 1.058824. A purported relative result inconsistent with those ratios has probably mixed percentages, denominators, dates, or adjustment conventions.

sections.title: A price ratio is not a momentum portfolio
paragraphs: The relative index above describes one matched price comparison. Jegadeesh and Titman instead rank a stock universe, form winner-minus-loser portfolios and specify formation and holding periods; in their 1965–1989 NYSE/AMEX sample those portfolios earned positive returns. That portfolio evidence does not validate buying this example’s leader. The research appendix keeps its market, comparator and cost assumptions visible.

example.title: Three end values, four distinct results
example.text: Stock 100→90 loses 10%; sector 100→85 loses 15%; market 100→80 loses 20%. Stock’s return advantage is 5 percentage points versus sector and 10 versus market. Relative-index gains are 90/85−1 = 5.8824% and 90/80−1 = 12.5%. Return differences and ratio changes use different denominators; neither transforms the stock’s loss into a gain.

exercise: From the main final values, calculate absolute returns, stock/market and stock/sector relative indices, and stock’s return differences against both comparators.

quiz.question: In the main final observation, which is the stock’s absolute return?
quiz.explanation: 90/100−1 is −10%; this is the holder’s price-only return.
feedback: Ten percentage points is its advantage over the falling market, not its own return.
90/100−1 is −10%; this is the holder’s price-only return.
12.5% is the market-relative ratio increase, using the market’s growth factor in the denominator.

outcomes: Rebase stock/comparator ratios and distinguish them from return differences.
Describe absolute loss alongside relative leadership.
Compare a stock with both sector and broad market under matched data conventions.
solution: Stock advantages are −10−(−20) = 10 percentage points and −10−(−15) = 5 points. Ratio gains are 12.5% and 5.8824%, not those percentage-point differences.

practice.title: Complete the session-6 note
practice.question: Use stock 96, sector 93, market 90 at session 6. Calculate both relative indices and write one sentence containing the absolute result.
solution: Stock/market = 100 × 96/90 = 106.6667; stock/sector = 100 × 96/93 = 103.2258. All initial values are 100.

Example note: “Stock is down 4% from the common start, but has outperformed sector and market in proportional terms, with relative indices 103.2258 and 106.6667.” Equivalent clear wording is acceptable.

practice.title: An absolute gain with relative weakness
practice.question: A separate stock rises $40→$44 while its benchmark rises 200→240. Calculate the rebased relative index and return difference.
solution: Stock factor 44/40 = 1.10; benchmark factor 240/200 = 1.20. Relative index = 100 × 1.10/1.20 = 91.6667. Relative-index change is −8.3333%.
Absolute stock gain is +10%; comparator gain +20%; return difference −10 percentage points. The stock gained value while losing relative ground.

evidence.claim: Research boundary: a specified stock momentum portfolio showed positive historical returns
evidence.location: Sections I–IV; Table III and market-model/transaction-cost paragraph, printed pp. 67–78, especially p. 77 (PDF page 14).
evidence.summary: Read the universe, formation/holding rules, benchmarks, and assumed cost adjustment.
evidence.limits: Historical cross-sectional portfolio evidence; distinct from a single stock/benchmark price ratio and not a current performance forecast. The study also reports that part of the first-year abnormal return dissipates over the following two years.

study.rule: Rank prior 3–12-month returns; long winners, short losers; hold 3–12 months in overlapping portfolios. Cost example: six/six months.
study.comparator: Winner-minus-loser spread and market-model risk adjustment; not a long-only stock account.
study.costs: Assumed 0.5% one-way cost, applied to observed turnover; no current retail cost estimate.
study.result: Positive sample returns; reported six/six-month risk-adjusted return after that cost: 9.29% annually.
